slides.text:
What is Machine Learning?
Machine Learning = Learning patterns from data to make predictions or decisions
• Instead of explicitly programming every rule, we provide data and a learning
algorithm.
• The system learns a model that maps inputs (features) to outputs (targets) or
decisions.
• Example: House area + location + rooms → predicted house price.
• Learning is evaluated on data that was not used to fit the model.
Intelligent Data Systems 1 | Machine Learning | 3

Types of Machine Learning
1. Supervised Learning 2. Unsupervised Learning 3. Reinforcement Learning
• Supervised: training examples contain input X and known target Y.
• Classification → predict a class/label.
• Regression → predict a continuous numerical value.
• Unsupervised: target labels are not provided; discover structure such as clusters.
• Reinforcement: an agent learns actions through rewards and penalties.
Intelligent Data Systems 1 | Machine Learning | 5

What is Regression?
• Regression is a supervised learning task in which the target variable is numerical
and typically continuous.
• The model learns a function that estimates Y from one or more input features X.
• Examples: predict house price, salary, sales, rainfall, temperature or energy
consumption.
• Goal: find a function that predicts well on unseen data.
X → Regression Model → Ŷ
Actual value y − Predicted value ŷ = Residual/Error

slides.text:
Linear Regression: Basic Idea
• Linear Regression models the relationship between input variable(s) and a
continuous target using a linear function.
• For one feature x, the model fits the best straight line through the observed data.
• The coefficients determine the intercept and slope of the line.
• The parameters are estimated by minimizing prediction error, commonly using least
squares. ŷ = b₀ + b₁x
b₀ = intercept | b₁ = slope/coefficient
Intelligent Data Systems 1 | Machine Learning | 10
• An intercept is the value of the predicted output y when the input x=0.
• Slope tells us how much the predicted Y changes when X increases by 1 unit.

Least Squares and Model Error
Sum of Squared Errors = SSE = Σᵢ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²
Residual = actual value − predicted value.
Squaring residuals prevents positive and negative errors from cancelling.
The fitted line is chosen to minimize the total squared error.
Common evaluation measures include MAE, MSE/RMSE and R².
Smaller error is desirable, but evaluation must use unseen/test data.

slides.text:
Linear Regression: Worked Example
Suppose study hours (x) are used to predict exam marks (ŷ).
Model: ŷ = 40 + 5x
For a student studying 6 hours: ŷ = 40 + 5(6) = 70 marks.
If the actual mark is 76, residual = 76 − 70 = +6.
x = 6 hours → ŷ = 70 marks
Interpretation: each additional hour is associated with an estimated +5 marks in this model.

slides.text:
Polynomial Regression: Why Do We Need It?
Real-world relationships are not always well represented by a straight line.
If the data show a curved trend, a polynomial model can capture that curvature.
A polynomial regression model adds powers of the input, such as x², x³, …
Although the curve is nonlinear in x, the model remains linear in its coefficients.
ŷ = b₀ + b₁x + b₂x² + … + bₖxᵏ
Degree 1 → straight line | Degree 2 → quadratic curve | Degree 3 → cubic curve
Intelligent Data Systems 1 | Machine Learning | 14

“GOODNESS OF FIT”
• Goodness of fit indicates how well a statistical or machine learning model explains the
observed data.
• A good-fitting model captures the underlying relationship between the input and
output variables.
• The difference between an observed value and its predicted value is called a residual.
• Smaller residuals generally indicate that predictions are closer to the observed values.
• Goodness of fit can be quantified using measures such as MSE and RMSE.
